q: A citizen posts peaceful criticism of a sarpanch's work. Consider: 1-Criticism alone is not incitement. 2-Defamation is a listed ground of restriction. 3-Maintenance of law and order is a listed ground. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Defamation is listed; law and order is not. Public order is the listed ground.
why: The eight listed heads include public order but not 'law and order', which is wider. Criticism does not become incitement merely because it is sharp.
trapnote: 'Law and order' never appears among the listed heads. Public order does. The two are not interchangeable.

q: A group is refused permission for an unarmed, peaceful meeting by an oral instruction with no law relied on. Which statement is correct?
options: The refusal is valid: assembly may be regulated on grounds of law and order
The refusal is valid: permission is a privilege and not a guaranteed freedom
The refusal fails: a restriction must rest on a law and satisfy reasonableness
The refusal fails: assembly is an absolute freedom admitting no restriction
expl: Restrictions must be by law and reasonable; an oral instruction with no legal basis fails both.
why: Two of the wrong options are attractive: assembly IS restrictable, but only by law and on listed grounds, and it is not absolute either.
trapnote: Ask two questions of every restriction: is there a law, and is the ground a listed one?

q: Consider the protection against ex post facto laws: 1-It bars conviction under a law not in force when the act was done. 2-It bars a penalty greater than that then prescribed. 3-It bars retrospective changes of procedure. Which is/are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: It reaches conviction and quantum of penalty, not procedural changes.
why: Procedure may be altered retrospectively; only the creation of the offence and the severity of the penalty are frozen as at the date of the act.
trapnote: The protection freezes the offence and the sentence, not the machinery by which a trial is conducted.

q: An accused is acquitted, and the State seeks a fresh prosecution on identical facts for the same offence. Separately a departmental inquiry proceeds on the same facts. Which statement is correct?
options: Both the fresh prosecution and the departmental inquiry are barred
The fresh prosecution is barred; the departmental inquiry may proceed
The fresh prosecution is permitted; the departmental inquiry is barred
Both are permitted, the bar applying only where a sentence was imposed
expl: The bar needs prosecution and punishment before a court; a departmental inquiry is neither.
why: The fourth option is the subtle one: the bar does require prosecution AND punishment, but an acquittal on the merits still bars a second prosecution for the same offence.
trapnote: Departmental and criminal proceedings run in parallel. Only a second court prosecution is barred.

q: Consider the protection against self-incrimination: 1-It extends to specimen handwriting. 2-It extends to a confession extracted by threat. 3-It applies only to a person accused of an offence. Which is/are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Handwriting is not testimony; a coerced confession is; and the protection needs an accused.
why: The protection covers what is drawn from the mind, not what is measured from the body. Fingerprints, blood and DNA also fall outside it.
trapnote: Body versus mind is the whole distinction. Anything compared rather than narrated falls outside.

q: A man is arrested at 6 pm Monday and produced before a magistrate at 9 pm Tuesday. Travel occupied four hours. Which statement is correct?
options: The requirement is breached: twenty-three hours remain after excluding travel
The requirement is satisfied: the period runs from the first working hour of the court
The requirement is satisfied: twenty-three hours remain after excluding travel
The requirement is breached: travel time forms part of the twenty-four hours
expl: Twenty-seven hours elapsed; deducting four hours of travel leaves twenty-three, within the limit.
why: Two options state the same arithmetic and differ only in the conclusion drawn, so the candidate must actually compute rather than recognise a phrase.
trapnote: Always subtract before concluding. Elapsed time minus journey is the figure that matters.

q: Consider the freedom to carry on trade: 1-It is available to citizens only. 2-It may be restricted by prescribing professional qualifications. 3-The State may carry on a trade to the complete exclusion of citizens. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: All three are correct; State monopoly is expressly saved.
why: The third is the one most candidates reject. A State monopoly, whether complete or partial, is expressly protected against challenge under this freedom.
trapnote: State monopoly is expressly saved. Rejecting it because it sounds extreme is the intended error.

q: A preventive detention order is made. Consider: 1-The detenu must be produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours. 2-The detenu has no right to legal representation before the Advisory Board. 3-Grounds of detention must be communicated. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Production before a magistrate belongs to the punitive track, not the preventive one.
why: The first statement imports the arrest timetable into preventive detention, where it has no application. Grounds and the absence of counsel are both correct.
trapnote: Two tracks, two sets of rules. Magistrate production and counsel belong to one of them only.

q: On the period of preventive detention without an Advisory Board opinion, which statement reflects the law in force?
options: Three months, the Board chaired by a person qualified to be a High Court judge
Two months, the Board chaired by a sitting judge of a High Court
Two months, the Board chaired by a person qualified to be a High Court judge
Three months, the Board chaired by a sitting judge of the Supreme Court
expl: The two-month change was enacted in 1978 but never brought into force; three months still governs.
why: The second option states a real constitutional amendment that was never notified. It is correct as text and wrong as law in force.
trapnote: An amendment that was passed is not necessarily an amendment in force. Three months is the operative figure.

q: A State law makes it an offence to publish material 'against the national interest'. Which is the strongest constitutional objection?
options: Speech may not be restricted by a State legislature, the power belonging to Parliament
Publication is protected absolutely, restrictions applying only to spoken utterances
'National interest' is not among the listed grounds on which speech may be restricted
Restrictions on speech require a prior proclamation of Emergency to be operative
expl: The listed heads are exhaustive; a ground outside them cannot save a restriction.
why: The heads are closed. Attractive-sounding grounds such as national interest, national security in that phrasing, or law and order do not appear.
trapnote: The eight heads are exhaustive. Any ground not on the list cannot be relied on however reasonable it sounds.

q: Consider the right to property: 1-It was omitted from Part III in 1978. 2-It is now a constitutional right outside Part III. 3-Its breach can be enforced directly by petition to the Supreme Court under the fundamental-rights remedy. Which is/are correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: It survives as a constitutional right, but the fundamental-rights remedy no longer lies for it directly.
why: The third statement is the trap: removing it from Part III necessarily removed access to the Part III remedy, though a High Court remedy remains available.
trapnote: Deletion from Part III removes the Part III remedy. The right survives; the route changes.

q: Compare Article 358 and Article 359 during a Proclamation of Emergency. Which statement is correct?
options: 358 requires an order and reaches all rights; 359 is automatic and confined to Article 19
358 is automatic and confined to Article 19; 359 requires an order and excludes Articles 20 and 21
Both operate automatically, and both are confined to war or external aggression grounds
Both require a Presidential order, and both exclude Articles 20 and 21 from their reach
expl: One suspends a right automatically on an external ground; the other suspends a remedy by order.
why: Each wrong option swaps one attribute only, so the candidate must hold four variables at once: trigger, instrument, scope and carve-out.
trapnote: Four variables distinguish these two provisions. Test each separately before choosing.

q: An officer records that an arrested person's relative was not informed because the station was short-staffed. Which statement is correct?
options: The requirement is mandatory; administrative difficulty is not a recognised excuse
The requirement is directory; substantial compliance during the inquiry suffices
The requirement applies only where the arrest is made without a warrant
The requirement applies only to arrests of women and of persons below eighteen
expl: Informing a nominated person is a mandatory safeguard now carried into statutory form.
why: The remaining options each narrow a general safeguard by inventing a qualification, which is how such distractors are usually built.
trapnote: Safeguards that protect liberty are read as mandatory. Look for options that quietly make them conditional.

q: Consider the progression of Article 21: 1-The 1950 view required only that some procedure exist. 2-The 1978 ruling required procedure to be fair, just and reasonable. 3-Privacy was recognised as part of the right in 2017. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: All three describe the accepted progression accurately.
why: Candidates often reject the first statement because it states an overruled position, but the statement is about what the 1950 view HELD, which is accurate.
trapnote: A statement describing a superseded holding is not thereby false. Read what the statement actually asserts.

q: A woman is to be arrested at 10 pm. Which statement reflects the correct position?
options: Arrest is barred after sunset in all circumstances without exception
Arrest requires the prior permission of a Sessions Judge after sunset
The restriction applies only where the offence is punishable with under seven years
Arrest is barred after sunset save with the prior permission of a Magistrate
expl: The safeguard is conditional, and the condition is prior permission of a Magistrate.
why: The second option converts a conditional safeguard into an absolute one, and the third moves the authority up a level. Both are common field misconceptions.
trapnote: Conditional safeguards are not absolute bars. Identify the authority and the condition precisely.

q: Consider the six freedoms as they now stand: 1-They are available to citizens only. 2-Freedom of the press is separately enumerated. 3-Each is subject to restriction on grounds specific to it. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Press freedom is not separately listed; it is read into freedom of speech and expression.
why: The second statement is the trap. The press has no distinct clause; its protection is derived, which is why restrictions on it run through the speech heads.
trapnote: Press freedom is derived, not enumerated. Expect it as a false statement in list questions.

q: A law provides that a person may be detained for two years without reference to an Advisory Board, Parliament having so prescribed. Which statement is correct?
options: Permissible: Parliament may prescribe the circumstances for detention beyond three months
Impermissible: no detention beyond three months is valid without a Board opinion
Permissible: any legislature may prescribe such circumstances for its own subjects
Impermissible: the maximum period of preventive detention is fixed at three months
expl: The Constitution expressly allows Parliament to prescribe classes of case for detention beyond three months.
why: Two options confuse the general rule with the express exception, and one confuses Parliament's exclusive competence with that of a State legislature.
trapnote: The three-month rule has an express exception exercisable by Parliament. It is a rule with a carve-out, not a ceiling.

q: Consider: 1-Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during an Emergency. 2-This was the position before 1978. 3-The judgment holding the contrary was expressly overruled in 2017. Which is/are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: The protection came in 1978; before that the contrary was held, and that holding was overruled in 2017.
why: The second statement inverts the chronology, which is exactly what makes the first and third appear to support it.
trapnote: Check whether a statement describes the position before or after the corrective amendment.

q: A procession is permitted but a participant carries a firearm. Which statement is correct?
options: The guarantee covers all assembly, arms going only to the reasonableness of restriction
The guarantee is lost for the entire procession once any participant carries a weapon
The guarantee applies, arms being permissible if licensed and carried openly
The guarantee covers assembly that is peaceable and unarmed; this falls outside it
expl: The guarantee is textually limited to assembly that is peaceable and without arms.
why: The third option overstates by penalising the whole assembly, and the fourth introduces a licensing qualification that the text does not contain.
trapnote: The limitation is in the text of the guarantee itself, not in the restriction clause.

q: On movement and residence: 1-Both may be restricted in the general public interest. 2-Both may be restricted to protect any Scheduled Tribe. 3-Both are available to every person in the territory. Correct?
options: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
expl: Both restriction grounds apply to both freedoms, but the freedoms belong to citizens alone.
why: The two restriction grounds are shared, which makes the third statement the only defect, and it turns on the rights-holder rather than the restriction.
trapnote: Shared restriction grounds tempt the eye away from the rights-holder. Check who holds the freedom.
